Pool-deck turf for two kinds of Altamonte Springs property

Turf around a pool or inside a lanai in Altamonte Springs runs $8–$18 per square foot as of September 2026. What changes the job more than the price is whether the pool sits on a single-family ranch lot or a condo's common element near Uptown Altamonte, since the two answer to different approval rules entirely.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A condo pool deck runs through a different rulebook

Several Uptown Altamonte and Cranes Roost-area buildings hold their pools as a common or limited common element rather than something an individual unit owner controls outright, and turf on that deck goes through the association's board under Florida’s Condominium Act rather than the single-family process the state's turf rule and HOA-visibility statute both describe. Neither of those two laws was written with a condo's shared pool deck in mind, since both apply specifically to single-family residential property.

Practically, that means a condo board's own rules, not a state floor, decide what a pool-deck turf project needs to clear before work starts. This is informational, not legal advice, and a specific building's declaration is the document that actually controls.

Older ranch pool cages need a different fix entirely

A 1970s or 1980s ranch home's screen-enclosed lanai is a single-family lot problem, not a condo one, and the turf question there is about drainage rather than approval process: turf laid over the enclosure's concrete deck needs a drainage underlay and glue-down edges rather than nails, since there's no soil underneath to anchor into. Pool and lanai turf inside an older screen cage also tends to run through narrower side strips than a newer enclosure, which changes how a crew seams the turf more than it changes the base.

Both jobs use the same product family; the deck itself dictates the install method. This post covers the underlay question for concrete, pavers and existing grass side by side.

Why washed rock matters most where concrete meets soil

Rainfall that hits a pool deck's concrete has nowhere to go but sideways, onto whatever soil border sits at the cage's edge, so a Altamonte Springs lot's washed, open-graded crushed rock does more work at that transition than it does in the middle of an open lawn. Unwashed fill would let fines settle and bind right where the extra volume arrives first, turning a narrow strip into the one part of the yard that stays soggy after every storm. The state's rule that subgrade material be washed before installation exists for exactly this kind of concentrated flow, not just ordinary rain falling evenly across a yard.

Confirming the drain point before infill goes down

Once the drainage underlay is glued to a Altamonte Springs lanai floor but before any infill goes in, the crew runs water across the surface to confirm it actually reaches the deck's existing drain rather than pooling in a low spot the underlay created by accident. Catching a flat or misdirected section at this stage means lifting a corner of underlay and reworking it, which is straightforward before infill is down and considerably more disruptive after. This check takes a few minutes and is the reason a finished lanai floor rarely surprises anyone with standing water months later.

A 6x40 ft strip inside a screened lanai

Say you have a 6x40 ft strip of turf planned for the two sides of a screened pool cage on a 1983 ranch home, 240 sq ft total, replacing grass that never filled in fully under the enclosure's shade. At $8–$18 per square foot, that's roughly $1,920–$4,320 installed, or $10–$16 a square foot for a typical build, closer to $2,400–$3,840. Because the strip sits over a concrete deck rather than soil, the quote adds a drainage underlay and adhesive-set edges rather than a standard rock base, and any irrigation head that used to reach that strip gets capped at the valve box as part of the same visit.

What does a small deck border cost, worked out?

Installed turf runs eight to eighteen dollars a square foot, typically ten to sixteen, and price does not change by Altamonte Springs ZIP code, only by access, base condition, and drainage. Say a homeowner wants a 250 sq ft strip between the pool cage and a side fence turfed rather than reseeded: at the typical range, that job runs somewhere between roughly twenty-five hundred and four thousand dollars, before accounting for anything unusual about the site. A quote well outside that range for a plain open border, high or low, is worth asking about specifically, since the underlying material and labor do not vary by neighborhood.

Reclaimed heads near a pool deck still get capped

A pool-cage yard on Altamonte Springs' reclaimed system often had a head or two watering the narrow strip just inside the screen, and that head gets capped at the valve box the same as any other once the strip is converted to turf, since the city’s reclaimed schedule stops applying to synthetic turf under the state's rule regardless of where the head sat. A crew checking a pool-deck job for old irrigation lines before laying turf avoids leaving one live under the new surface by accident.

A clogged deck drain from infill that migrated the wrong way

Infill that washes off a Altamonte Springs pool border and into the deck's own drain can back the drain up enough that water starts sheeting across the border after storms that used to clear fine, turning what started as a turf maintenance issue into standing water against the coping. Because the drain itself is shared with the pool deck's runoff generally, tracing the cause back to turf infill rather than a pool-deck plumbing problem can take longer than it should. A border sloped toward a drain is worth checking for infill buildup at the drain grate specifically, not just for thinning infill across the turf itself.

Brushing the crossing point between the loungers and the ladder

The stretch of turf that gets crossed barefoot between a set of loungers and the pool ladder mats down faster than any other section of a Altamonte Springs deck border, since it carries more repeated foot traffic in a single afternoon than the rest of the yard sees in a week. Brushing that crossing against the grain every few weeks keeps the blades standing instead of laying over permanently along the worn path. A section further from the water, along a side fence, rarely needs the same attention since almost nobody walks it directly.

Questions people ask

Does a condo pool deck near Cranes Roost need HOA-visibility approval under F.S. 720.3045?

No. That statute covers a single-family homeowners association's declaration; a condo's common and limited common elements run through Florida's Condominium Act and the building's own declaration instead, which is a separate approval path with its own board.

Can turf go over an existing concrete pool deck inside a screen cage?

Yes, with a drainage underlay beneath it and the edges set with adhesive rather than nails, since there's no soil at that point to anchor into. The rest of the yard, if any, can still use a standard compacted rock base.
